title: Persecuted (Matthew 5:10–12)
hook: blessed when you're insulted for doing right

segments.voice: Yesterday, the peacemakers: people who build peace where there wasn't any. Did you take one small step toward a peace? Day two hundred forty.

Think of the time you did the right thing and it cost you. You spoke up for someone and got frozen out of the group. You told the truth and lost the deal. You refused to laugh at the joke and became the next joke. Doing right doesn't always get applause. Sometimes it gets you punished. The last of the Beatitudes is the one nobody puts on a coffee mug. After the empty-handed, the mourners, the meek, the hungry, the merciful, the pure and the peacemakers, Jesus blesses the people who get hurt for it.
screen: `IT COST YOU.` → `THE NEXT JOKE.` → `THE LAST BEATITUDE.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." Listen to that ending. Theirs is the kingdom of heaven. It's the same promise as the very first beatitude, the poor in spirit. The list opens and closes with the same words, like bookends. Everything in between lives inside the kingdom. And notice: for righteousness' sake. Not for being difficult, or rude, or right in an annoying way. For doing what's right. Then Jesus turns and speaks straight to the people in front of him, not they any more but ye: blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake. And then the strangest instruction in the sermon: "Rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in heaven: for so persecuted they the prophets which were before you." The Greek word for be exceeding glad is agalliasthe. It's more than smiling through it. It's the word for jumping for joy. Why rejoice? Not because pain is good. Because you're in good company: the prophets walked this road before you. The book of Acts tells how the apostles, after being beaten, left rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer for his name. Christians have been persecuted in many times and places, from the first centuries to today, and people of many faiths know that suffering too. For many Christians, this beatitude has been less a theory and more a lifeline: whatever happens, it isn't the end, and you're not alone.
screen: `THE SAME PROMISE AS THE FIRST.` · `FOR RIGHTEOUSNESS' SAKE.` · `AGALLIASTHE: JUMP FOR JOY.` · `IN GOOD COMPANY: THE PROPHETS.` · then, large: `REJOICE, AND BE EXCEEDING GLAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember Christians who suffer for their faith today. Settle, and breathe. Around the world, some Christians face prison, violence or losing their homes for what they believe. Picture one of them: a pastor in a cell, a family that had to flee, a teenager mocked at school for praying. If you pray, you can pray for them now, by name if you know one. If you don't pray, simply hold them in mind, and wish them courage and safety. The bell holds the time.
Persecuted. The last beatitude: blessed are those hurt for doing right, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
Your line: rejoice anyway. Today, if doing right costs you something small, notice it, and remember you're in good company. Day two hundred forty.

howItsDone: Christians remember martyrs on their feast days, and many churches set aside a day or a Sunday each year to pray for Christians who are persecuted around the world.

fork.setup: you're one of the disciples on the hillside. Jesus says people will insult you and lie about you for his sake. what does he tell you to do?
fork.reveal: "Rejoice, and be exceeding glad." not because pain is good, but because the prophets walked the same road.

original.note: Greek: be exceeding glad, leap for joy. Matthew 5:12.

trapdoor: what you thought: blessed are those who suffer.
what it means: blessed are those hurt for doing right: theirs is the kingdom, and they're in the prophets' company.
what a scholar hears: theirs is the kingdom of heaven frames verses 3 and 10, bracketing the eight beatitudes.

notes: The practice follows the outline ('pray for Christians suffering today'), phrased as an invitation, with a non-praying option. No countries named, to avoid ranking or politics; a Keeper may wish to add specifics.
Matthew 5:11 is echoed in the voice with KJV wording ('revile you, and say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake') but not cited as a quotation; confirm or add as a quoted source.
agalliao as 'jump/leap for joy': common rendering; confirm.
The inclusio (5:3 and 5:10) is standard. Some count nine beatitudes (with 5:11); the script avoids a count except 'the eight' in the trapdoor.
International Day of Prayer for the Persecuted Church (November, in many churches): confirm howItsDone phrasing.
